# The Reality War
"The Reality War" is the eighth and final episode of the fifteenth series of the British science-fiction television programme Doctor Who. It was first broadcast on BBC One on 31 May 2025, and was released simultaneously via Disney+ in international markets. The episode was written by Russell T Davies (the series showrunner) and directed by Alex Pillai. Serving as the series finale, "The Reality War" concludes a two-part story begun in the previous episode "Wish World". It features the Fifteenth Doctor, portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, alongside companion Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu), in an adventure that brings back classic Doctor Who villains the Rani (played by Archie Panjabi) and Omega. The episode is notable for its climactic regeneration scene in which Gatwa’s Doctor sacrifices himself and transforms into a new incarnation with the face of former companion Rose Tyler, portrayed in a surprise twist by Billie Piper. It also includes a brief cameo by Jodie Whittaker, reprising her role as the Thirteenth Doctor, marking her first appearance on the show since 2022.
## Plot
Following the events of "Wish World," the Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) and Belinda Chandra find themselves in a fabricated alternate reality created by tech mogul Conrad Clark and sustained by the renegade Time Lord Rani (Archie Panjabi). The Rani’s plan is to destabilize reality on Earth in May 2025 – repeatedly resetting 23 May 2025 to prevent 24 May from arriving – as part of a scheme to weaken the fabric of the universe. This “reality war” is intended to facilitate the return of Omega, an ancient, exiled Time Lord, whom the Rani hopes to use to rebuild their destroyed home planet Gallifrey and resurrect the Time Lord race. Meanwhile, the Doctor struggles with a personal crisis: in the Wish World reality, he and Belinda unwittingly have a young daughter, Poppy, whose existence defies normal Time Lord biology. Knowing that destroying the false reality will erase Poppy from history, the Doctor becomes determined to save her even as the universe hangs in the balance.
As the finale unfolds, the Doctor works to break his friends and allies out of the Wish World illusion. He frees former companion Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson) and UNIT leader Kate Lethbridge-Stewart (Jemma Redgrave) from the spell, restoring their memories of him. Together, they confront the Rani and her past self, the aged Mrs. Flood (Anita Dobson), who had “bi-generated” into two bodies to further her plans. The Rani reveals her intent to use Omega’s power to seed a new generation of Time Lords, circumventing the infertility caused by Gallifrey’s demise. Belinda and the Doctor place Poppy inside a specially constructed Zero Room – a shielded chamber existing outside normal reality – to protect the child from the impending destruction of the fake world.
The conflict comes to a head when the Rani succeeds in opening a gateway to the Underverse, allowing Omega to emerge. Omega appears as a towering skeletal leviathan, having been monstrously deformed by eons trapped in an anti-matter universe. In a swift and chaotic turn of events, the gigantic Omega snatches up the Rani and devours her whole, abruptly eliminating the very villain who engineered his return. (The Rani’s older iteration, Mrs. Flood, manages to escape using a Time Ring device.) Almost as quickly, Omega himself is dispatched: the Doctor seizes a conveniently placed Gallifreyan weapon called the Vindicator and fires it at Omega, banishing the primordial Time Lord back into the void almost instantaneously after his arrival. With the “unholy trinity” of antagonists (the two Ranis and Omega) defeated as reality collapses, the Doctor and Ruby race back to the TARDIS. They reopen the Zero Room and are relieved to find Belinda and baby Poppy alive, apparently having survived the dissolution of the Wish World.
Back in the restored real timeline, the heroes’ relief is short-lived. Without warning, Poppy vanishes from the TARDIS and from everyone’s memory – everyone except Ruby, who remembers the child and realizes something is wrong. It becomes clear that Poppy’s survival is a paradox; reality has “snapped back” after the Wish World’s end, erasing the half-Time Lord child from history. Ruby pleads with the Doctor to save his daughter, reminding him that he was willing to do anything to prevent Poppy from being written out of existence. Determined to set things right, the Doctor resolves to make the ultimate sacrifice. Alone in the TARDIS, he devises a desperate solution: he will unleash his regeneration energy directly into the Time Vortex to “punch a hole” between realities and realign history so that Poppy can exist.
At that moment, the Doctor is unexpectedly joined by a projection of one of his former selves – the Thirteenth Doctor (Jodie Whittaker) – who appears inside the TARDIS due to the temporal schism caused by reality’s instability. She gently warns the Fifteenth Doctor of the extreme danger in what he’s about to do, cautioning that using regeneration energy in this manner could destroy the Time Vortex and unravel reality. The Fifteenth Doctor, however, insists that saving Poppy is worth the risk. In a brief but heartfelt exchange, the two Doctors share a moment of understanding (lightly joking in unison about things being “timey-wimey”) and acknowledge the pain of letting go. Accepting that this is his only path, the Fifteenth Doctor bids the Thirteenth farewell as she fades away, and he proceeds with his plan.
The Doctor releases a massive burst of regeneration energy into the TARDIS console, tearing open a controlled rift in space-time. He is last seen standing in the TARDIS doorway, golden energy pouring from his body out into the cosmos as he forces reality to shift. The scene then transitions to a quiet garden in the early morning: the Doctor awakens on the lawn of Belinda’s home to discover that history has been altered. Poppy is alive and well – now purely human, born to Belinda and an ordinary human partner in this timeline. Belinda is overjoyed to be reunited with her daughter at last, and the Doctor is content that they are safe. He realizes that in this rewritten reality he is no longer Poppy’s father, but simply “Uncle Doctor,” as Belinda always intended to return to this date to reunite with her child. After a tender goodbye, Belinda chooses to stay behind and raise Poppy, parting ways with the Doctor for the sake of her child’s normal life.
With his companion gone and his goal accomplished, the Doctor returns to his TARDIS alone. Reflecting on the “absolute joy” of his recently ended incarnation, he acknowledges that his time has come to an end. The Doctor triggers the regeneration process in solitude, releasing energy as his TARDIS hurtles through space. In the final moments of the episode, the Doctor’s face and body change mid-regeneration, revealing an astonishing new form. He has taken on the appearance of Rose Tyler – the Doctor’s former companion from two decades prior – now apparently regenerated as the next Doctor. The newly transformed Doctor, with Rose’s face (Billie Piper), looks into the camera with a wide grin and cheerily greets, “Oh, hello!”, leaving the nature of this transformation and the character’s identity a tantalizing mystery as the series concludes on a dramatic cliffhanger.
## Background and Production
### Development and returning characters
"The Reality War" served as the grand finale for Doctor Who’s 2024–25 season (marketed as Series 15 in the UK, and as "Season 2" of the revived show on some platforms). Showrunner Russell T Davies, who wrote the episode, crafted it to be both a high-stakes spectacle and a personal farewell for the Fifteenth Doctor. In the lead-up to broadcast, Davies teased that the story would “shake up the lore of Gallifrey” and take some “unexpected turns”, recontextualizing the relationship between the Doctor and the Rani. As head writer, Davies drew on elements of Doctor Who mythology not seen on television in decades. Omega’s return is a significant example: the ancient Time Lord antagonist had last appeared in 1983, and Davies decided to reinvent the character for the modern era. He explained that the events of the Last Great Time War allowed him to “tweak the legend” of Omega and update the character’s backstory, effectively “reinventing” the villain while respecting the series’ long history. In "The Reality War", Omega is depicted in a radically new form – a towering, corpse-like entity – reflecting his corrupted state after centuries trapped in an interdimensional void. Longtime fans noted that this was Omega’s first active role in a Doctor Who story since Arc of Infinity (1983), making his inclusion a notable callback to the classic era.
The episode also features the return of the Rani, another classic-era character. The Rani (a renegade Time Lord scientist) had not appeared on-screen since 1987, and her reintroduction in modern Doctor Who was foreshadowed throughout Series 15. In "The Reality War", the character is portrayed in a dual form: Archie Panjabi guest-stars as the Rani’s younger self, while veteran actress Anita Dobson appears as “Mrs. Flood,” revealed to be an older incarnation of the Rani. This plot device – referred to in dialogue as “bi-generation” – allowed the Rani to coexist in two bodies at once, effectively having two versions of the same Time Lord present simultaneously. The concept provided a unique twist on regeneration lore and gave the finale two villainous figures for the Doctor to contend with (nicknamed the “two Ranis”). Davies and the production team coordinated closely with Doctor Who Magazine to keep details of the Rani’s dual casting under wraps until broadcast.
The regular cast for "The Reality War" included Varada Sethu as new companion Belinda Chandra, who had been introduced earlier in Series 15. This episode marked the culmination of Belinda’s character arc, which centered on her hidden backstory and maternal drive. It also saw the brief return of Millie Gibson as former companion Ruby Sunday, who had departed the TARDIS in the previous season; Gibson’s appearance allowed Ruby to play a role in the resolution of the story. Additionally, several past characters from both modern and classic Doctor Who made cameo appearances in the episode’s climax, reflecting the broad scope of the finale’s narrative. Notably, Jemma Redgrave reprised her recurring role as UNIT chief Kate Lethbridge-Stewart, Bonnie Langford appeared as Melanie “Mel” Bush (the 1980s companion, integrated into the story via the Wish World scenario), and Yasmin Finney had a brief cameo as Rose Noble (a character from the 60th anniversary specials). These cameos tied together various eras of the show’s lore as reality unraveled in the plot.
### Filming and secrecy
Production of "The Reality War" took place in late 2024 under conditions of intense secrecy, due to the spoiler-sensitive nature of the story’s ending. The episode was directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai, whose prior work on the series included other high-concept episodes in the Fifteenth Doctor’s era. Pillai oversaw large-scale action set-pieces, such as the confrontation with Omega’s giant form – accomplished through a mix of practical effects (a massive creature prop was reportedly used on set for certain shots) and CGI enhancements. Scenes set in the surreal “Wish World” were filmed with stylized visuals to distinguish the alternate reality, and archive footage of past Doctors (Jon Pertwee and Matt Smith) was cleverly integrated into one sequence where the character Anita searches through time for the Doctor. Composer Murray Gold provided the musical score, which incorporated leitmotifs from earlier seasons to underscore the many callbacks in the finale.
The production team went to great lengths to conceal the episode’s major twists from leaking. In particular, Jodie Whittaker’s cameo as the Thirteenth Doctor was kept top-secret. To avoid any mention of Whittaker’s name during shooting, she was listed under the codename “Petrol” on call sheets and script drafts. Her scenes were likely filmed in closed sets with minimal crew. Whittaker’s brief return was the first time an outgoing Doctor from the previous era returned for a cameo in their successor’s finale, drawing deliberate parallel to how past Doctors have occasionally guided their future selves (as seen in 2013’s "The Day of the Doctor", for example).
The regeneration scene at the end of "The Reality War" was one of the most closely guarded secrets in modern Doctor Who history. Unlike most Doctor regenerations in the 21st century, which are typically announced by the BBC well in advance, Ncuti Gatwa’s departure was not confirmed publicly before broadcast. This marked an unprecedented move – it was the first time in the “NuWho” era that a Doctor’s regeneration came as a complete surprise to the audience on the night of airing. To achieve this, the production likely filmed multiple decoy endings and took precautions during editing. Billie Piper’s involvement was arranged at the last minute and similarly shrouded in secrecy. Piper, who famously played companion Rose Tyler in 2005–2006, was brought in to film the regeneration payoff with minimal notice, ensuring the news wouldn’t leak. In the end credits of the episode, the BBC even chose not to list her as “The Doctor” – instead crediting her appearance simply as “Introducing Billie Piper”. This coy credit left the exact nature of her role ambiguous and heightened fan speculation. According to Piper, she was approached “very last-minute” to shoot the surprise scene, highlighting the production’s agile efforts to secure the cameo once the decision was made. The finished regeneration sequence, showing Gatwa’s Doctor morphing into Piper, was filmed in strict secrecy and not included in advance screenings for reviewers, in order to preserve the shock value.
### Broadcast and release
"The Reality War" aired on BBC One in the UK at 6:50 pm BST on 31 May 2025, in the programme’s traditional Saturday evening slot. Uniquely, the BBC did not release this finale episode on iPlayer on the morning of broadcast (a practice they had experimented with for earlier episodes of the series); instead, the finale was held for a synchronized evening premiere to prevent spoilers from emerging during the day. Internationally, the episode was made available on the same date via Disney+, as part of a special co-production and distribution deal for the series. The finale’s anticipated popularity also led to an event-style release: "Wish World" and "The Reality War" were screened back-to-back in select cinemas across the UK on 31 May 2025, giving fans a chance to watch the two-part finale on the big screen. This theatrical double-bill mirrored the previous year’s approach for the Series 14 finale and was accompanied by fan screenings that reportedly sold out in some locations.
Accompanying the episode’s broadcast, the BBC aired a teaser for an upcoming spin-off titled The War Between the Land and the Sea, a five-part series starring Russell Tovey which continues the broader story universe. This spin-off’s trailer was shown immediately after "The Reality War", serving to bridge the gap during the show’s hiatus. Notably, Doctor Who was approaching a period of uncertainty at the time of the finale’s airing. The BBC had not yet officially announced a full new series beyond the episodes already produced with Disney, which led to media speculation about the show’s future. The shock ending of "The Reality War" – with its game-changing regeneration – thus came at a pivotal moment. Some industry observers interpreted the bold cliffhanger as a statement of confidence. TV critic Scott Bryan commented that the Billie Piper reveal felt “like a pitch to Disney to say: ‘Hi, please renew us, we’ve got Billie Piper’”. In August 2025, the BBC publicly reassured fans that Doctor Who would continue, confirming a new Christmas special for 2026 written by Davies and indicating that the show was not ending despite the pause in production.
## Reception
"The Reality War" received a mixed reception from critics and fans, with widespread astonishment at its ending but divided opinions on its storytelling. On its night of broadcast, the episode garnered an overnight audience of 2.2 million viewers on BBC One. This was a modest figure by Doctor Who’s historical standards, yet it ranked as the second most-watched TV programme of the day in the UK (trailing only the Britain’s Got Talent final). Consolidated ratings (which include catch-up and streaming over the following week) rose to approximately 3.4 million viewers. These numbers represented a slight boost from the preceding weeks – indeed, "The Reality War" became the second highest-rated episode of the series after its penultimate installment – but they also underscored the general decline in Doctor Who’s viewership during 2025. Earlier episodes in May had fallen below 3 million, marking the lowest audience levels of the modern era. The finale’s ratings uptick and high drama did generate renewed buzz, though it was apparent that the show was struggling to regain the broad audience it enjoyed in previous years.
Critical reviews of the episode highlighted its ambitious scope and shocking climax, while debating the effectiveness of its narrative. Den of Geek described the finale as ending the season in a “strange, unsettling place,” noting that the episode was “mind-boggling” in the sheer amount of plot threads it tried to resolve. The review praised the boldness of the creative decisions but expressed bafflement at certain storytelling choices – especially the handling of companion Belinda. Commentators pointed out that Belinda, ostensibly the Doctor’s co-lead throughout the season, is largely sidelined in the finale’s second half (at one point literally sealed away in a box), which Den of Geek called “one of the most bewildering decisions that Russell T Davies has made” in terms of character use. Similarly, The A.V. Club’s recap argued that the episode felt like two halves awkwardly stitched together: one half hurriedly wrapping up the season’s plot about the Wish World and its villains, and the other half dedicated to the Doctor’s regeneration spectacle. The result, according to A.V. Club critic Isobel Lewis, was that the much-hyped adversaries – the Rani and Omega – were dispatched “almost instantly”, undermining the threat that had been built up, while the regeneration overshadowed the resolution of the story’s core conflict. Some reviewers and fans found humor or disappointment in how quickly Omega, teased as the Doctor’s “greatest ever enemy”, was defeated after such a long absence.
On the other hand, the surprise regeneration twist was widely praised for its audacity and shock value. Both critics and viewers acknowledged that Doctor Who managed to pull off a genuine surprise in an age of constant media leaks. The Guardian reported that there was “an audible gasp” in live fan screenings when Billie Piper appeared on screen, and many were impressed that the BBC had successfully kept her return a secret. The moment of the Fifteenth Doctor transforming into a form resembling Rose Tyler immediately set off fervent discussion and speculation. Publications like Inverse and Radio Times dissected the ending, questioning whether Piper is truly playing the next Doctor or if there is a deeper “timey-wimey” explanation (such as the Bad Wolf entity or a reality glitch) for her presence. The ambiguity of her on-screen credit (not explicitly calling her “the Doctor”) fueled theories that the story might be more complex than a straightforward regeneration.
Fan reaction ranged from exhilaration to skepticism. Longtime viewers who grew up with Rose Tyler were thrilled by the nostalgic callback and intrigued by the bold re-casting of Piper in a new role. “I think Billie Piper is fantastic... one of the reasons the 2005 series landed so well,” said TV critic Scott Bryan, emphasizing the iconic status she brings. However, others were more critical. Some fans voiced concern that the show was relying too heavily on past characters at the expense of original ideas. “You want something new... bringing back characters loses its novelty if you keep doing it,” one viewer remarked, worrying that the twist, while surprising, might indicate creative stagnation if not handled carefully. This debate over nostalgia versus innovation became a talking point in the fandom after the finale. Meanwhile, many lamented the premature end of Ncuti Gatwa’s tenure. Gatwa’s performance as the Doctor had been widely lauded, and his exit after just two series made his run one of the shortest in the show’s history. Fans and critics alike noted that Gatwa’s Doctor had “unfulfilled potential” and that they “wish we had longer” with him – a sentiment even echoed in the episode’s dialogue during the poignant farewell between the Doctor and his former self.
Despite these critiques, "The Reality War" succeeded in generating substantial buzz and curiosity about the future of Doctor Who. The dramatic cliffhanger ensured that discussions continued well beyond the broadcast, with mainstream media covering Piper’s unexpected return and the unanswered questions it raised. In retrospect, reviewers noted that the finale’s strengths lay in its emotional beats and the performances: Ncuti Gatwa’s exuberant portrayal received praise up to the end, and his final scenes (particularly the heartfelt interaction with Jodie Whittaker’s Doctor and the sacrificial goodbye to Belinda and Poppy) were highlighted as touching and well-acted. Murray Gold’s soaring musical score during the regeneration sequence and the visual spectacle of the Doctor’s energy blasting into the cosmos were also commended for their cinematic flair.
Overall, "The Reality War" is remembered as a bold and polarizing finale. It delivered one of the most startling endings in the show’s history, capping off a season that experimented with the format (alternate realities, secret companions, and unorthodox release strategies) while also struggling with viewership challenges. The episode’s legacy largely hinges on its final minutes: the unprecedented regeneration into a familiar face, which left audiences both amazed and anxious to see how this reality-bending twist will be resolved in subsequent specials. In the months after airing, the BBC confirmed that Doctor Who would return to address the cliffhanger – with a 2026 Christmas special announced, ensuring that the mysteries of "The Reality War" (and the fate of Billie Piper’s character) would eventually reach a payoff. In the meantime, "The Reality War" stands as a showcase of Doctor Who’s willingness to take risks with its long-established formula, underlining the series’ enduring capacity to surprise and reinvent itself even after more than 60 years on air.

The regeneration scene at the end of "The Reality War" was one of the most closely guarded secrets in modern Doctor Who history.
Unlike most Doctor regenerations in the 21st century, which are typically announced by the BBC well in advance, Ncuti Gatwa’s departure was not confirmed publicly before broadcast.
This marked an unprecedented move – it was the first time in the “NuWho” era that a Doctor’s regeneration came as a complete surprise to the audience on the night of airing.
To achieve this, the production likely filmed multiple decoy endings and took precautions during editing.
Billie Piper’s involvement was arranged at the last minute and similarly shrouded in secrecy.
Piper, who famously played companion Rose Tyler in 2005–2006, was brought in to film the regeneration payoff with minimal notice, ensuring the news wouldn’t leak.
In the end credits of the episode, the BBC even chose not to list her as “The Doctor” – instead crediting her appearance simply as “Introducing Billie Piper”.
This coy credit left the exact nature of her role ambiguous and heightened fan speculation.
According to Piper, she was approached “very last-minute” to shoot the surprise scene, highlighting the production’s agile efforts to secure the cameo once the decision was made.

The finished regeneration sequence, showing Gatwa’s Doctor morphing into Piper, was filmed in strict secrecy and not included in advance screenings for reviewers, in order to preserve the shock value.
"The Reality War" aired on BBC One in the UK at 6:50 pm BST on 31 May 2025, in the programme’s traditional Saturday evening slot.

Uniquely, the BBC did not release this finale episode on iPlayer on the morning of broadcast (a practice they had experimented with for earlier episodes of the series); instead, the finale was held for a synchronized evening premiere to prevent spoilers from emerging during the day.
Internationally, the episode was made available on the same date via Disney+, as part of a special co-production and distribution deal for the series.

The finale’s anticipated popularity also led to an event-style release: "Wish World" and "The Reality War" were screened back-to-back in select cinemas across the UK on 31 May 2025, giving fans a chance to watch the two-part finale on the big screen.
This theatrical double-bill mirrored the previous year’s approach for the Series 14 finale and was accompanied by fan screenings that reportedly sold out in some locations.

Accompanying the episode’s broadcast, the BBC aired a teaser for an upcoming spin-off titled The War Between the Land and the Sea, a five-part series starring Russell Tovey which continues the broader story universe.
This spin-off’s trailer was shown immediately after "The Reality War", serving to bridge the gap during the show’s hiatus.
Notably, Doctor Who was approaching a period of uncertainty at the time of the finale’s airing.
The BBC had not yet officially announced a full new series beyond the episodes already produced with Disney, which led to media speculation about the show’s future.
The shock ending of "The Reality War" – with its game-changing regeneration – thus came at a pivotal moment.
Some industry observers interpreted the bold cliffhanger as a statement of confidence.
TV critic Scott Bryan commented that the Billie Piper reveal felt “like a pitch to Disney to say: ‘Hi, please renew us, we’ve got Billie Piper’”.

In August 2025, the BBC publicly reassured fans that Doctor Who would continue, confirming a new Christmas special for 2026 written by Davies and indicating that the show was not ending despite the pause in production.
"The Reality War" received a mixed reception from critics and fans, with widespread astonishment at its ending but divided opinions on its storytelling.
On its night of broadcast, the episode garnered an overnight audience of 2.2 million viewers on BBC One.
This was a modest figure by Doctor Who’s historical standards, yet it ranked as the second most-watched TV programme of the day in the UK (trailing only the Britain’s Got Talent final).
Consolidated ratings (which include catch-up and streaming over the following week) rose to approximately 3.4 million viewers.

These numbers represented a slight boost from the preceding weeks – indeed, "The Reality War" became the second highest-rated episode of the series after its penultimate installment – but they also underscored the general decline in Doctor Who’s viewership during 2025.
Earlier episodes in May had fallen below 3 million, marking the lowest audience levels of the modern era.
The finale’s ratings uptick and high drama did generate renewed buzz, though it was apparent that the show was struggling to regain the broad audience it enjoyed in previous years.
Critical reviews of the episode highlighted its ambitious scope and shocking climax, while debating the effectiveness of its narrative.
Den of Geek described the finale as ending the season in a “strange, unsettling place,” noting that the episode was “mind-boggling” in the sheer amount of plot threads it tried to resolve.
The review praised the boldness of the creative decisions but expressed bafflement at certain storytelling choices – especially the handling of companion Belinda.

Commentators pointed out that Belinda, ostensibly the Doctor’s co-lead throughout the season, is largely sidelined in the finale’s second half (at one point literally sealed away in a box), which Den of Geek called “one of the most bewildering decisions that Russell T Davies has made” in terms of character use.

Similarly, The A.V. Club’s recap argued that the episode felt like two halves awkwardly stitched together: one half hurriedly wrapping up the season’s plot about the Wish World and its villains, and the other half dedicated to the Doctor’s regeneration spectacle.

The result, according to A.V. Club critic Isobel Lewis, was that the much-hyped adversaries – the Rani and Omega – were dispatched “almost instantly”, undermining the threat that had been built up, while the regeneration overshadowed the resolution of the story’s core conflict.
Some reviewers and fans found humor or disappointment in how quickly Omega, teased as the Doctor’s “greatest ever enemy”, was defeated after such a long absence.
On the other hand, the surprise regeneration twist was widely praised for its audacity and shock value.
Both critics and viewers acknowledged that Doctor Who managed to pull off a genuine surprise in an age of constant media leaks.
The Guardian reported that there was “an audible gasp” in live fan screenings when Billie Piper appeared on screen, and many were impressed that the BBC had successfully kept her return a secret.
The moment of the Fifteenth Doctor transforming into a form resembling Rose Tyler immediately set off fervent discussion and speculation.

Publications like Inverse and Radio Times dissected the ending, questioning whether Piper is truly playing the next Doctor or if there is a deeper “timey-wimey” explanation (such as the Bad Wolf entity or a reality glitch) for her presence.
The ambiguity of her on-screen credit (not explicitly calling her “the Doctor”) fueled theories that the story might be more complex than a straightforward regeneration.
Fan reaction ranged from exhilaration to skepticism.
Longtime viewers who grew up with Rose Tyler were thrilled by the nostalgic callback and intrigued by the bold re-casting of Piper in a new role.
“I think Billie Piper is fantastic... one of the reasons the 2005 series landed so well,” said TV critic Scott Bryan, emphasizing the iconic status she brings.
However, others were more critical.
Some fans voiced concern that the show was relying too heavily on past characters at the expense of original ideas.

“You want something new... bringing back characters loses its novelty if you keep doing it,” one viewer remarked, worrying that the twist, while surprising, might indicate creative stagnation if not handled carefully.
This debate over nostalgia versus innovation became a talking point in the fandom after the finale.
Meanwhile, many lamented the premature end of Ncuti Gatwa’s tenure.
Gatwa’s performance as the Doctor had been widely lauded, and his exit after just two series made his run one of the shortest in the show’s history.

Fans and critics alike noted that Gatwa’s Doctor had “unfulfilled potential” and that they “wish we had longer” with him – a sentiment even echoed in the episode’s dialogue during the poignant farewell between the Doctor and his former self.
Despite these critiques, "The Reality War" succeeded in generating substantial buzz and curiosity about the future of Doctor Who.
The dramatic cliffhanger ensured that discussions continued well beyond the broadcast, with mainstream media covering Piper’s unexpected return and the unanswered questions it raised.

In retrospect, reviewers noted that the finale’s strengths lay in its emotional beats and the performances: Ncuti Gatwa’s exuberant portrayal received praise up to the end, and his final scenes (particularly the heartfelt interaction with Jodie Whittaker’s Doctor and the sacrificial goodbye to Belinda and Poppy) were highlighted as touching and well-acted.
Murray Gold’s soaring musical score during the regeneration sequence and the visual spectacle of the Doctor’s energy blasting into the cosmos were also commended for their cinematic flair.
Overall, "The Reality War" is remembered as a bold and polarizing finale.

It delivered one of the most startling endings in the show’s history, capping off a season that experimented with the format (alternate realities, secret companions, and unorthodox release strategies) while also struggling with viewership challenges.

The episode’s legacy largely hinges on its final minutes: the unprecedented regeneration into a familiar face, which left audiences both amazed and anxious to see how this reality-bending twist will be resolved in subsequent specials.

In the months after airing, the BBC confirmed that Doctor Who would return to address the cliffhanger – with a 2026 Christmas special announced, ensuring that the mysteries of "The Reality War" (and the fate of Billie Piper’s character) would eventually reach a payoff.

In the meantime, "The Reality War" stands as a showcase of Doctor Who’s willingness to take risks with its long-established formula, underlining the series’ enduring capacity to surprise and reinvent itself even after more than 60 years on air.

Escaping through a doorway into the time-travelling holiday destination, Anita explains that the hotel is becoming unstable due to the Rani’s constant repetition of May 23rd, 2025. With real time restoring his memories fully, the Doctor and Anita return to the Wish World to ensure the safety of [Belinda](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/belinda-chandra) and [Poppy](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/poppy). While [the Rani](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-rani) and [Mrs Flood](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/mrs-flood) prepare the final stage of their plan to find [Omega](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/omega), the Doctor and Anita bring the Time Hotel doors to UNIT Tower; where the flow of real time restores the memories of [Kate Lethbridge-Stewart](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/kate-lethbridge-stewart), [Colonel Ibrahim](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/colonel-christofer-ibrahim), and everyone else on duty. Kate wakes up [Ruby Sunday](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/ruby-sunday), [Shirley Bingham](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/shirley-bingham) and [Mel Bush](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/mel-bush) using their UNIT bio-chips. As the team assembles, the Rani confronts the Doctor in UNIT HQ, where she reveals her plan is to use Omega’s body as a gene bank to begin a new race of Time Lords. The Doctor insists that Poppy’s existence is proof that there is another way to achieve her goals without need of the Mad God. Returning to the Bone Palace, the Rani sets the [Bone Beasts](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/bone-beasts) on UNIT Tower to prevent them from interfering in her plan, as UNIT Tower becomes an active battle station in response to the threat. As battle rages, the Doctor and [Susan Triad](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/susan-triad) build a Zero Room to protect Poppy from the effects of [Conrad Clark](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/conrad-clark)’s wish. Determined to protect her daughter, Belinda enters the Zero Room with Poppy. The Doctor and Ruby both make their way to the Bone Palace to confront the Rani and Conrad respectively. The Doctor arrives just as the Rani executes her final plan, opening a doorway for Omega to enter from the Underverse. The original Time Lord emerges – now a hulking, decaying titan. Declaring himself as a God of Time, Omega snatches up the Rani and eats her whole. As Mrs Flood makes her escape using the Rani’s Time Ring, the Doctor is left to face the Mad God alone. Grabbing the stolen Vindicator, the Doctor blasts Omega with a powerful beam that drives him back into the Underverse, ending the titan’s threat. Using an Indigo Device, Ruby teleports to Conrad to face her ex-boyfriend once more. Failing to appeal to his better nature, Ruby tricks Conrad by teleporting behind him and grabbing the baby [Desiderium](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/desiderium). She makes her own wish for Conrad to be happy and he disappears. As Ruby ends the wish that created this reality, she finds herself and the baby inside the Doctor’s [TARDIS](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-tardis). Returning to UNIT, the Doctor is delighted to find that both Belinda and Poppy emerge from the Zero Room unscathed. Not knowing where Desiderium came from, the Doctor and Ruby bring the baby to [Carla](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/carla-sunday) and [Cherry Sunday](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/cherry-sunday); who take the child in as one of their own, naming the child Joseph Sunday. Bringing Poppy to the TARDIS, the Doctor and Belinda plan where they want to go next – but Poppy disappears as they speak, leaving Ruby as the only person who can remember her. At UNIT, the TARDIS team discover that since the end of the wish, there are a few permanent changes to reality – and Conrad Clark is alive and well, with no memory or record of who he was before. Ruby pleads to the Doctor to remember and find Poppy, who she believes is lost in the cracks of time. Determined not to lose an innocent life, the Doctor leaves his companions behind and departs in the TARDIS. Knowing his next action will cost him his life, the Doctor prepares to sacrifice himself; but is suddenly interrupted by one of his predecessors, the [Thirteenth Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/thirteenth-doctor)! She has appeared in the TARDIS as a result of a “giant time schism” that the Doctor is about to cause. Unable to talk him out of his plan, the Doctor offers her future self some words of wisdom and comfort before returning to her own time. The Doctor then triggers a release of his regeneration energy and targets it on the TARDIS console, creating the schism in the Time Vortex. The Doctor wakes up in a garden, where he is reunited with Belinda and to his delight, Poppy. Time has re-aligned itself, Poppy has survived and remains Belinda’s daughter - however, she now has a human father instead of the Doctor. Belinda reminds "Uncle Doctor" that she was _always_ trying to get back to May 24th at 7:30am, to pick up Poppy. Satisfied that they are both safe and happy, the Doctor bids both Belinda and Poppy farewell. Seeking company, the Doctor takes the TARDIS in view of the star that was once his friend, [Joy Almondo](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/joy-almondo). June 19, 2025

The writer speaks to Doctor Who Magazine about ‘tweaking the legend’ to bring back the deadliest Time Lord of them all…

Amongst the challenges the [Fifteenth Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/fifteenth-doctor) faced in his final episode, [_The Reality War_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-reality-war), was the return of yet another dangerous Time Lord – [Omega](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/omega), the “first Time Lord”, last seen in 1983’s [_Arc of Infinity_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/arc-of-infinity). After spending some time trapped in the Underverse, Omega has ascended beyond his humanoid form, into a great godlike creature surrounded in myth – which not even [the Rani](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-rani) was fully prepared to face!

Speaking to _Doctor Who Magazine_, showrunner and episode writer Russell T Davies discusses the legend of Omega, and how he reworked the character using the show’s pre-existing backstory…

**Issue 618 of** _**Doctor Who Magazine**_ **is on sale now.** [**You can order it here.**](https://doctorwhomagazine.com/subscriptions/)

![Image 1: Omega Reality War](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-06/DWTV-Gallery-Module-Watermark-Template-4cb2a9ced6.jpg)

**Russell T Davies on bringing back Omega…**

"At one point, I sat there thinking I’d invent a new Time Lord… I thought I would create a Time Lord nobody has ever heard of, who was banished. But then that simply just becomes a shorthand for Omega. I love the fact that, as fans, discuss this show and that it must be new, and must move forward. And within another ten words, we mention the Rani! You have to accept that it’s a 62-year-old show, and this is part of its vocabulary.

"I used the Time War to tweak the legend of Omega. A lot of things said about Omega were not said in the original series. You have to accept that 40 years have passed. The Time War came along and everyone’s history got changed. So that’s what Omega is now. You can reinvent it.

"Our way of walking through the world is constantly being re-analysed. So I like to think it’s the same on Gallifrey. That’s happened, over the eons, Omega has been recontextualised, and the story gets bolder and changes over time. We don’t want to repeat the past, we want to push it forward…"

‘An audible gasp’: Doctor Who fans shocked by Billie Piper return
=================================================================

This article is more than 6 months old

Actor who played Rose Tyler pops up at a pivotal time for the series as Ncuti Gatwa bows out, creating a vacancy

[Harry Taylor](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/harry-taylor)

Sun 1 Jun 2025 19.08 BSTLast modified on Mon 2 Jun 2025 02.30 BST

[Share](mailto:?subject=%E2%80%98Anaudiblegasp%E2%80%99:DoctorWhofansshockedbyBilliePiperreturn&body=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2025/jun/01/an-audible-gasp-doctor-who-fans-shocked-by-billie-piper-return?CMP=share_btn_url)

Nearly two decades since she first appeared on Doctor Who, Billie Piper made a spectacular return to the show on Saturday night, in the latest season’s [finale, The Reality War](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2025/jun/01/doctor-who-reality-war-ncuti-gatwa-varada-sethu-anita-dobson-recap). After just two series, Ncuti Gatwa’s Doctor regenerated into a grinning Piper, who greeted viewers with a “oh Hello!” in the episode’s final scene.

The 42-year-old is best known to [Doctor Who](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/doctor-who) fans for playing the Doctor’s companion Rose Tyler for two seasons when the show was reintroduced to TV screens in 2005 after a 16-year break.

Her return came as a genuine shock to fans, many of whom were impressed that the [BBC](https://www.theguardian.com/media/bbc) had managed to avoid leaks. But it has also left them with questions – will Piper play the Doctor in the show’s next series? And will there be a next series at all?

In February the [BBC denied reports the show faced the axe](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-not-cancelled-bbc-response-newsupdate/) – but said any decision wouldn’t be made until the latest series had been broadcast. Its statement pointed out half of the 26 episodes agreed with Disney+ still had not aired. Twenty-one out of those 26 have now aired, leaving a five-episode spinoff starring Russell Tovey, the trailer for which aired after Saturday’s finale.

TV critic and Doctor Who fan Scott Bryan, 35, said the reintroduction of Piper to the show came at a pivotal time for Doctor Who, amid speculation about its future. “I think it felt a bit like, towards the end of the episode, a pitch to Disney to say: ‘Hi, please renew us, we’ve got Billie Piper’.”

“Of course we’ve not had any confirmation about whether the Disney deal will be renewed, but also when or if these episodes will be aired. Nothing has been confirmed regarding filming. It’s a moment in TV that has raised more questions than answers, but that’s how Doctor Who works.”

Concerns have been raised about falling viewing figures, which have struggled to rally since Russell T Davies’ return in 2023. Two episodes during this series, which aired in May, got less than 3 million viewers – the lowest since the modern era began airing in 2005.

[Doctor Who finale sees Ncuti Gatwa depart in surprise regeneration Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2025/may/31/doctor-who-ncuti-gatwa-russell-t-davies)

The coordinator of the Doctor Who Appreciation Society, Tony Jordan, 66, from Staffordshire, said he was concerned about the show’s future. “Obviously if it had been a stellar success then they would have recommissioned it already,” he said.

“It is a concern that it is not going straight back into production but, to be fair, there have been times since it came back in 2005 where you’ve had a year-long break.”

Whether Piper will play her old character Rose, the Doctor or another character is also unclear. The credits, which showed Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker as “the Doctor” did not do the same for Piper.

Christopher Eccleston, who starred alongside her as the Doctor, [told an event in the US in 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=jKEiPliikhu_5SEF&v=QZDoJ9k0o0U&feature=youtu.be) he backed the idea of his former assistant taking on the role.

He said: “I was saying to somebody today in the green room that Russell T Davies is coming back, right, and who’s going to be his Doctor? I think it should be Billie Piper actually. Catherine Tate’s great but, I think there’s your Doctor.”

Dan McLaughlin, 30, who was watching the finale with fellow fans at a cinema in Manchester when Piper appeared said: “There was an audible gasp when she came on, definitely. There was maybe about two or three cheers, and someone behind me swore.”

Bryan said: “It was a real surprise. I think Billie Piper is fantastic, she was one of the reasons why the 2005 series landed so well and led to 20 years of a hugely successful show and a reboot. But a surprise nonetheless.”

He added: “I’m intrigued by what they decide to do with her, and the fact that there’s mysteries around the fact that we don’t know whether she’s playing the Doctor, it’s a bit open ended.”

McLaughlin said he felt “deflated” by Piper’s appearance as it indicated a lack of new ideas behind the show.

He said: “Billie Piper’s amazing and Rose was a wonderful character, but you want something new now, you want to be excited. I loved \[David\] Tennant in the 60th anniversary special, but bringing back characters loses its novelty if you just keep on bringing the old ones back all the time. It’s lacking in original ideas.”

93.content:
A [_Doctor Who_](https://www.avclub.com/doctor-who-recap-season-2-episode-6) season finale is normally a pretty predictable beast. At least in the NuWho era, we could expect the eventual defeat of a major villain, some revelation about the Doctor’s past, and humanity being saved by our Time Lord hero. Yet I clicked play on “The Reality War” with questions hanging in the air that far transcended the show’s plot.

No, the real query on the lips of fans—or at least fans who have been paying attention to tabloid reports and online speculation—is whether Ncuti Gatwa would still be in the TARDIS by the time the end credits rolled. Such an option felt unprecedented. Gatwa has only appeared in two seasons of the show (most modern Doctors have done three), but more significantly, never before has a Doctor’s regeneration not been officially announced in advance.

There’s little point speculating on the reasons and logistics behind Gatwa’s exit—not here, at least. But I will say this: This is very clearly an episode of two halves. There is the continued story from last week and there is the regeneration. Even with the episode stretched to 67 minutes instead of the normal 45, the former feels incredibly rushed and makes all the same mistakes as last season’s finale, “Empire Of Death”. We’re told the Doctor is about to face his greatest ever enemy, only for them to be destroyed almost instantly. At that, you can only laugh.

Initially, the episode’s start is well-paced. Rather than May 24, 2025 finally arriving in the Wish World, May 23 keeps repeating, which the Doctor warns is part of the Rani’s plan to weaken reality and eventually allow the most fearsome Time Lord in existence, Omega, to return. The Doctor, however, is struggling to get his head around the fact that now he and Belinda (Varada Sethu) have a daughter in former space baby Poppy. Initially, Belinda doesn’t even remember the Doctor, but once he’s thrown off his John Smith getup and takes out the kilt, it all comes flooding back.

One by one, the Doctor rescues his former companions and colleagues from the Wish World’s spell, snapping them out of this false reality and reminding them who he is. The UNIT team reunion, however, is rudely interrupted by the Rani (Archie Panjabi). This steely villain requires little range from Panjabi, but the actor is clearly having so much fun in the role that it’s hard to care.

The Rani reveals her plan to the Doctor: to rebuild Gallifrey, their destroyed home planet. A brief explanation for what the hell bigeneration is ensues, and the Doctor explains that Time Lords are infertile and unable to continue their race. “Sometimes I think that’s what bigeneration is,” he says. It also could explain Poppy’s existence. Perhaps she is the Doctor’s own longing for a child brought to life.

But his love for this extremely cute kid raises one big problem. In order to defeat the Rani, they must destroy the Wish World, which would lead to Poppy no longer existing. Belinda, whose maternal instinct is so strong that it appears to have overridden any other character development, is willing to do it all for her daughter. Against the Doctor’s wishes, she goes with Poppy into a specially built cell that exists outside of their reality. In theory, anything inside this heavily enclosed room should survive this destruction of the Wish World. But if it doesn’t work, they would be stuck in there forever—and not existing.

The first emotional goodbye between the Doctor and Belinda follows, before the Doctor and Ruby (Millie Gibson) launch a two-pronged attack on the Rani’s lair. Ruby goes for Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King), the creator of the Wish World who has been surprisingly absent from this episode. She confronts her former boyfriend/current foe (who among us doesn’t have one of those?) and learns that he’s had some kind of unexplained change of heart where he really does want to help people, thanks to the Doctor.

The Doctor, meanwhile, finds the Rani and Mrs. Flood and for reasons unclear takes them up on their offer to see Omega. The door to the underworld opens, and a terrifying claw the same size emerges. Out crawls a real feat of design: a huge skeletal monster with a hollow chest, sunken eyes and a cavernous mouth. Near instantly, he picks up the Rani and swallows her whole, marking a particularly unfitting ending for Panjabi’s long-teased villain. Mrs. Flood makes a dash for it, surviving yet again.

Yet Omega doesn’t even last as long as the Rani. The Doctor grabs hold of his very own Chekhov’s gun—the vindicator hanging on the wall behind him—and blasts this creature back into the underworld. After all that buildup, this monster gets less than three and a half minutes of airtime. And there we were saying that Sutekh was a wasted opportunity…

Around the Doctor, the bone palace begins to disintegrate. The Doctor races to find the TARDIS and Ruby inside, and back with their friends, they learn with relief that Belinda and baby Poppy have somehow both survived the end of the Wish World. They celebrate, while the Doctor and Belinda excitedly babble to Ruby about their plans to travel the universe together with their daughter.

Everything seems so…happy. But Ruby knows something is wrong. When she turns around, Poppy’s cot is empty, her questioning met with two terrifying words: “Who’s Poppy?” Outside, no one from UNIT remembers her either. It’s suggested that Ruby’s memory could be one of the minor glitches that occurred when they recreated this reality, but Ruby won’t let it go. Poppy was real; the Doctor was once willing to do anything to make sure that she wasn’t written out of history, so he should do it again for his own daughter.

“We’re missing one person,” the Doctor agrees, as the orchestral arrangement swells. UNIT offers to help, but the Doctor insists only the last of the Time Lords can do this. What that actually means becomes clear when the Doctor is alone in the TARDIS, repeating Poppy’s name to himself—and then: “Oh, man. I like this face.” Yep, it’s regeneration time, baby!

Before then, we get a truly unexpected surprise. The Doctor’s past faces play on the TARDIS’s screen, but then the Thirteenth Doctor, Jodie Whittaker herself, is there in the space ship with him. There’s something truly tender about their interactions, as they say the words “timey-wimey” in unison and cackle. “All these faces and we never really change,” Whittaker’s Doctor says.

In the lead-up to his regeneration, Gatwa’s performance is infused with disappointment but a real sense that it’s his time to go. Fans, who never got to see Gatwa battle a Dalek or Cyberman, will likely feel differently. And you can sense the show, and Gatwa himself, addressing them directly in the episode’s most moving moment. “I wish we had longer,” he tells Whittaker, to which she replies: “We always wish that.” It’s a smart way of acknowledging the fans without patronizing them.

Solitary once more, the Doctor’s palms glow with their tell-tale sign of regeneration. He aims them towards the TARDIS, then wakes up with his face on the lawn of a house we’ve never seen before. There’s a reason for that. This is the colorful home Belinda has been begging to get back to all season. Although this time, she’s there with Poppy, who has clearly survived thanks to the Doctor. And in this timeline, the Doctor isn’t Poppy’s father. No, a quick sonic screwdriver scan confirms that this little girl is 100-percent human, the product of Belinda and an ex named Richie she is still on good terms with.

His work having succeeded, it’s time for the Doctor to say goodbye to both mother and daughter. I do find it disappointing seeing Belinda simply reduced to a parental role, yet her decision to leave the Doctor and not put her daughter at risk is understandable. “I hope you’ll see me again…but not like this,” he tells her and closes the TARDIS door. The Doctor is on his own, and we all know what that means. For once, he acknowledges it. “I don’t want to do this alone,” he says and runs across the TARDIS, the lights going out behind him one row at a time. The Doctor flings open the doors and looks out at the universe that has always been here for him. “Joy to the world,” he shouts, “and this has been an absolute joy.”

So it’s here: the big regeneration moment. The Doctor throws his head back, and beams of light erupt from his body and spread across the galaxies. To start with, I really thought the scene would cut to black before the next Doctor could be revealed. After all, casting rumors are usually swirling for months before a regeneration. But this one is unexpected in every way. In those final moments, Gatwa’s face is replaced with one fans know well: a twitching, then giddily grinning Rose Tyler, the former companion played by Billie Piper.

**Stray observations** 
-----------------------

*   • How did you react when you saw Rose and heard her say “oh, hello”? Shriek in excitement? Groan in despair? Personally, I went for that most British of responses: an audible “bloody hell.” Frankly, I think it’s too early to offer a response to Piper’s return. Whether she’s the full-on next Doctor, or simply sticking around for a little while, remains to be seen. We likely won’t get answers for a while anyway. Spin-off _The War Between The Land And See_ is on its way, but new _Doctor Who_ episodes will be a long time coming.
*   • For now, I’ll try not to let these questions about the show’s future overshadow Gatwa’s exit (even though his regeneration arguably overshadowed any semblance of a storyline in this episode). He has been a wonderful Doctor in the face of ridiculous criticism, and brought a freshness to the character I hope will be taken forward. Like many fans I wish he’d stayed longer, but I also totally understand why it may have been his choice to just do two seasons rather than hold out years for the next batch of episodes.

“Timey wimey” doesn’t even begin to describe the Season 2 finale of _Doctor Who_. “The Reality War” brought the season’s long-running mystery — the Earth mysteriously being destroyed suddenly on May 24, 2025 — to its conclusion, but introduced a last-minute twist that saw the end of Ncuti Gatwa’s 15th Doctor, and the return of a _very_ familiar face. But what does it all mean? Is the 15th Doctor really gone? Is the 16th Doctor really who she seems to be? Let’s dig into the wild, twisty ending of “The Reality War.”

**Spoilers ahead for _Doctor Who_’s “The Reality War.”**

Doctor Who “The Reality War” Ending Explained
---------------------------------------------

The crux of the episode’s late climax, and the reason for the 15th Doctor’s regeneration, is the existence of Poppy.

BBC

“The Reality War” picks up with “Wish World’s” very literal cliffhanger by having the Doctor saved from his fall by Anita (Steph de Whalley), the hotel receptionist with whom the Doctor spent a whole year during the [2024 Christmas special](https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/doctor-who-paradox-joy-to-the-world-big-bang). But Anita’s gotten a promotion to be the manager of the Time Hotel, which gives her access to a key that can open a door to any time. The time of May 24, 2025, however, is causing the Time Hotel to spasm, as the fate of Earth on this day puts the Hotel and its entire structure at risk of collapse. With Anita’s help, the Doctor breaks UNIT out of their Wish World-induced haze, and brings Belinda and their daughter Poppy back to the UNIT headquarters to wage war against [the Rani](https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/who-is-the-rani-mrs-flood-archie-panjabi-doctor-who) (Archie Panjabi), Mrs. Flood aka also the Rani (Anita Dobson), and Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King).

The Rani’s plan, it turns out, is to bring Omega back to create a new Gallifrey — and she needs him to create the blueprint for a new Time Lord race, as the Master’s destruction of Gallifrey and genocide of its people left the surviving Time Lords (aka the Rani and the Doctor) infertile. Though the existence of Poppy throws a wrench in this whole explanation and scheme, the Doctor points out, as she shouldn’t be able to be created from his DNA. But she is real, and he and Belinda (Varada Sethu) are determined to make sure she will exist after the Wish World is destroyed, with the Doctor tasking Susan Triad (Susan Twist) with building a Zero Room in which Belinda and Poppy can be kept safe from the disintegrating reality.

And when the Rani and Omega are defeated by the Doctor (at alarming speed, thanks to a giant, zombified Omega eating Rani and the Doctor’s conveniently-placed Vindicator), their plan seems to have worked: they open the Zero Room, and out steps Belinda with a still-real Poppy. But when the Doctor returns with Belinda, Poppy, and Ruby (Millie Gibson) to the TARDIS, Ruby notices something odd happen: Poppy disappears, and the Doctor and Belinda don’t seem to remember her. When she tearfully pleads with the Doctor to save Poppy — who appears to have been a victim of “time shifting by one degree” — the Doctor jumps into the TARDIS with plans to use his regeneration energy to punch a hole into the time vortex and shift reality into its proper place. That’s when the first familiar face pops up.

Jodie Whittaker makes a brief cameo as the 13th Doctor, to warn the 15th Doctor about the dangers of punching a hole in the time vortex.

BBC

Jodie Whittaker’s 13th Doctor appears in the TARDIS, thanks to a “schism in time” caused by reality snapping back in place after the disintegration of the Wish World. She warns the 15th Doctor not to use his regeneration energy, as it could destroy the time vortex and all of reality — but concedes quickly as he tells her of the life at stake. (Side note: Whittaker has never been better than in these brief minutes written by Russell T Davies, one wishes her dialogue was as good as this in her era.) She heads off to _not_ confess her love to Yaz, and the 15th Doctor prepares to blow a hole in the time vortex.

Suddenly, he wakes in the backyard of Belinda’s home and learns that Poppy is not his daughter, but only Belinda’s — a few inserted scenes of Belinda talking about Poppy throughout their adventures reveal that she had a daughter all along — and that’s why she was so desperate to get home. Happy that Belinda is reunited with the daughter she was desperate to return to, the Doctor heads off to finish his regeneration... and that’s when the biggest twist of the episode happens.

Billie Piper as the 16th Doctor?
--------------------------------

The 15th Doctor regenerates at the end of this episode, with his face bursting into light and turning into... Billie Piper’s. “Oh, hello!” she says as she recognizes her new face.

That’s right, the actress who played the 9th (Christopher Eccleston) and 10th Doctor’s (David Tennant) companion, Rose Tyler, is back but as the Doctor. And yes, that means that Ncuti Gatwa’s 15th Doctor is gone: Gatwa confirms in this behind-the-scenes [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dz-35CJcgCc) that his [era as the Doctor is over](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/ncuti-gatwa-says-final-farewell-to-the-tardis-as-the-fifteenth-doctor-regenerates). It feels like a shame that his era ends after two seasons (making his run as the Doctor one of the shortest in the history of the show), especially after the 15th Doctor finally felt like he was [coming into his own with Season 2](https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/doctor-who-season-2-review-bbc-disney-plus). But we’re given little time to grieve his departure, with the reveal of the next Doctor — or is she?

Billie Piper as Rose Tyler_._

BBC

But is Billie Piper really the 16th Doctor? Tinfoil hat theory time: In the credits, we see “Introducing Billie Piper,” but notably _not “_as the Doctor.” Could there still be ripple effects left from the reality shift caused by the disintegration of the Wish World? Is this another “glitch,” as UNIT calls the handful of other discrepancies? Or maybe she’s playing “Bad Wolf,” as she did in the 50th anniversary special, “The Day of the Doctor”? And does this mean Russell T Davies is building up to a very awkward reunion between Tennant’s 14th Doctor and Piper’s Doctor?

Who knows if we will find out soon, as [_Doctor Who_’s future on Disney+ remains unknown](https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/doctor-who-new-showrunner-rumor). The only thing confirmed to be coming next in the Whoniverse in the [_The War Between the Land and the Sea_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoM7pfpE3u0) [spinoff](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoM7pfpE3u0), but it’s clear that the main show is building up to something big again. Or maybe it’s just another [nostalgia ploy to keep the show afloat](https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/doctor-who-review-the-star-beast-60th-anniversary-special). At the very least, _Doctor Who_ does what it does best: it leaves us bewildered, and oddly emotional, but always wanting more.

![Image 1](https://www.denofgeek.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Stefan-Mohamed-author-pic-1.jpg?fit=200%2C166&resize=200%2C200&filter=grayscale) | June 1, 2025 |

| [Comments count:0](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-15-episode-8-review-the-reality-war/#disqus_thread)

![Image 2: Ncuti Gatwa in a blue denim suit and white t-shirt in the TARDIS](https://www.denofgeek.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/The-Reality-War-Doctor-Who-Ncuti-Gatwa.jpg?resize=768%2C432)

_Photo: BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon_

**Warning: contains spoilers for _Doctor Who_ episode “The Reality War.”**

In _Doctor Who_’s frankly mind-boggling season finale, the Doctor’s epic battle with [the two Ranis](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-solves-mrs-flood-mystery-post-credits-scene-explained/), [Omega](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-returning-classic-era-villain-explained/), Conrad and a herd of skyscraper-sized bone creatures ultimately comes down to the restoration of a single life – and will require a sacrifice nobody expected. Spoilers ahead.

It’s honestly difficult to know where to start with this episode. There are so many potential jumping-off points for discussion – though, somewhat tellingly, very few of them relate to the actual story that kicked off in earnest last week, which the episode itself seems positively impatient to get out of the way. It takes about 15 minutes for the Doctor to stop hugging every member of the extended supporting cast so the titular war can kick off, then by the halfway mark it’s over. Audacious? Yes, though that’s not to say it actually works.

Do we start with [Billie Piper](https://www.denofgeek.com/billie-piper/)? Or the unexpected and quite charming Jodie Whittaker cameo? Or the fact that they somehow snuck Ncuti Gatwa’s regeneration onto the screen without anybody knowing?

No, because this season didn’t start with Billie Piper, or Jodie Whittaker, or the Rani, or Ruby Sunday. It didn’t even start with the Doctor. It started with Belinda Chandra. A character with so much potential – compassionate, uncertain, a little bit spiky, competent in a new and interesting way, compellingly distrustful of the Doctor.

Potential that has, at this point, been mostly wasted.

There is a point in “The Reality War” where Belinda basically tells the Doctor “OK I think I’m done contributing to this episode, good luck tho” and is left holding the baby in a soundproofed box where she can neither affect or be affected by the story happening outside. We even have an unintentionally comical cut back to her standing in there, doing nothing, saying nothing. It’s hard to think of a more literal way to sideline a key player. This is the co-lead of the show! The companion! And instead of having any real agency, instead of contributing to the plot in any meaningful way whatsoever, she functionally stops existing as a narrative presence. She doesn’t even get to go with the Doctor when he rushes off to save what turns out to be _her_ child.

And for what? So that the companion who supposedly left the show last season can have all the big dramatic moments instead?

There were no advanced screeners available for this episode – given what happens at the end, it’s easy to see what they were scared might leak – so I’m writing with less distance than usual, reacting fairly rapidly to a first watch. But even with several days to digest, it’s difficult to imagine feeling anything other than bafflement at this storytelling choice. _This_ is what Belinda’s whole story arc was leading to? _This_ is the big twist? It’s truly one of the most bewildering decisions that Russell T Davies has made. It already kind of felt like he’d run out of meaningful stuff for Belinda to do after “The Well”, and there have been plenty of complaints about her sidelining in “[Wish World](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-15-episode-7-review-wish-world/)”, but nobody could have predicted this.

Sorry Belinda. And sorry Varada Sethu. You both deserved better.

Now to Ncuti Gatwa. It’s pointless getting into behind-the-scenes gossip, or speculating on the actor’s motivations – if he only ever wanted to do two seasons, of course that’s his choice. But what are we to take away from his brief tenure in storytelling and character terms? A Doctor defined by his joy, his exuberance, his love for people (frustratingly, a point this episode hammers until it becomes tedious). A smile as powerful as a billion supernovas. A killer wardrobe. Even in lesser episodes, Gatwa’s energy has carried us along, infectious and delightful. It’s a genuine shock and a shame to see him go.

Not least because, as with Belinda, it feels like his Doctor had unfulfilled potential. Was this episode truly a satisfying conclusion to Fifteen’s story? He gets plenty of good moments, big and small, and of course he plays the hell out of all of them. You could argue that sacrificing their life to save one child is about the most Doctor-ish thing possible. I wouldn’t necessarily argue with you.

But that’s broad strokes stuff, generally applicable to any incarnation. What about _this_ Doctor makes _this_ specific set of circumstances a fitting send-off? Is it satisfying for this Doctor, a Doctor representing a particular streak of joyful hedonism, a Doctor who releases UNIT from their stifling roles in Conrad’s reactionary wish world via an explicit and triumphant assertion of his queerness, to go out in this way, for these reasons? It just doesn’t feel like that’s what these past two seasons – the bi-generation, his relationship with Rogue, his torturing of Kid, the seemingly forgotten Susan stuff – have been leading to.

It’s a shame that the episode also feels so messy on a minute-to-minute level. There are individually effective moments – _Dark Souls_ boss Omega is a fantastic visual, and him casually munching The Rani is enjoyably WTF (though I can’t help wishing they’d offed the other one and kept Archie Panjabi around). The moment with the Doctor and Belinda passing Poppy’s jacket back and forth and folding it until it vanishes is kind of jaw-dropping in how understated and upsetting it is. Anita’s first joke about being in hospitality is funny (the second and third iterations not so much). Millie Gibson does a great job, even if it feels like a misstep to give Ruby so much heavy lifting to do instead of Belinda. But the whole thing feels so all over the place that not even Gatwa’s megastar energy can hold it together.

And now he’s gone, regenerated into Billie Piper. At this point, we have no idea when the show will be back. It’s impossible to know where this is going. And it’s hard not to feel torn – on the one hand, [Billie Piper is a fantastic actor](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/the-best-tv-performances-of-billie-piper/), and it’s fascinating to consider what her take on the role will be (though it should be noted that the credits pointedly don’t say “Billie Piper as The Doctor”, whatever that could mean – [we ponder a few theories here](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/who-is-that-big-returning-doctor-who-star-playing/)).

On the other hand, didn’t we just do this? We had the second Tennant Doctor, it was a lovely gift for fans that wrapped up some loose ends and gave everyone a big warm glow for the anniversary, and then we flew off with Ncuti Gatwa, an actor who couldn’t have screamed more loudly that things were going to be _different._

But now we’re looking backwards again. And as fun a surprise as Piper’s appearance is, as fully as she will no doubt own the role… it feels like another retrograde move. It’s _Doctor Who_ celebrating itself, getting lost in its own mythos, turning inward.

And so we end this oh-so promising season in a strange, unsettling place. An episode that doesn’t really seem to care that much about the story it claimed to be telling, which makes discussing it seem weirdly beside the point. A show in limbo. A whole incarnation of the Doctor gone, when we’d barely started to get to know him. A promising companion wasted. A showrunner everyone expected to be a safe pair of hands making some utterly confounding choices.

Where do we go from here?

_[Doctor Who](https://www.denofgeek.com/doctor-who/) series 15 is available to stream now on BBC iPlayer in the UK and on Disney+ around the world._
